prisoner.name: Roberto E. Rivera
prisoner.description:
Roberto Epifanio Rivera was a New York-licensed physician living in Ridgewood, New Jersey, who died of COVID-19 in New Jersey custody on April 22, 2020, aged 68 — seven years, five months and six days after his arrest, and none of it spent at liberty.

Ridgewood police arrested him on November 16, 2012 after a search of his apartment turned up bomb-making chemicals — nitric acid in a basement freezer, along with hydrogen peroxide, glycerin, sulfuric acid, calcium hypochlorite and potassium perchlorate — as well as roughly ten pounds of thermite, trigger mechanisms, disguises, and two Cobray M11 assault weapons. Bail was set at $1 million cash. He did not make it, and was held at the Bergen County Jail in Hackensack for the six years his case took to come to trial.

He was never charged with an active plot to bomb anything, and contemporary reporting said so plainly at the time. Prosecutors argued at trial that his interest in explosives followed his involvement with Occupy Wall Street in about August 2011, and that he had described contemplating placing explosives beneath the Charging Bull statue in the Wall Street financial district. The convictions were for what was in his apartment, not for anything he did with it.

His connection to Occupy is not a simple one. Contemporary reporting described him as a vocal supporter who volunteered medical care to protesters, and a neighbour recalled seeing him carrying protest signs. Immediately after the arrest, a member of the Occupy Wall Street press team said he knew of no connection between Rivera and the movement, and stressed its commitment to nonviolence.

A jury convicted him in December 2018 of possessing the explosive materials, acquitted him of creating a risk of widespread harm, and hung on two weapons counts. A second trial convicted him on the weapons charges on January 18, 2019, and he was sentenced on February 22, 2019 to 25 years in New Jersey state prison. As COVID-19 moved through the state's prisons he was considered for emergency release; prosecutors objected, and he stayed inside. He died six weeks later.

keep_case.charges: Possession of explosive materials and unlawful possession of assault firearms — bomb-making chemicals, roughly ten pounds of thermite, trigger mechanisms and two Cobray M11 assault weapons found at his Ridgewood, New Jersey apartment on November 16, 2012. He was not charged with an active plot to bomb anything.
keep_case.convicted: Yes — convicted in December 2018 of possessing the explosive materials, acquitted of creating a risk of widespread harm, with the jury hung on two weapons counts; convicted on the weapons charges at a second trial on January 18, 2019.
keep_case.sentence: 25 years in New Jersey state prison

delete_case_matching.reason: The spurious row. It says arrested and incarcerated November 15, 2012 and released April 21, 2020, at MCC Chicago, with no charge and no conviction. Every part of it is wrong: the arrest was the 16th, the institution is a federal jail in Illinois on a New Jersey state prosecution, and he was never released -- he was being considered for emergency release around that date and died in custody the following day. That last error is the worst thing on the record, because it turns a death into a release.

flags_note: in_custody false and released FALSE, which looks odd until you read Prisoner::getIncarcerationYearsArray. It tests died-in-custody as (! released && death_date), and its comment names the same state recorded for Luis Rodriguez and Romaine Fitzgerald: both flags off, death date set. Marking him released would be both untrue and would break the stats chart, which would then stop counting his years at an unrecorded release instead of at his death.
duration_note: death_in_custody_date on the case rather than only death_date on the prisoner. The saving hook on PrisonerCase mirrors it into release_date, so imprisoned_for_days stops at the death and computes 2,714 days -- seven years, five months, six days -- instead of running to today. That is what replaces the 14 years 11 months the record was showing.
birthdate_note: 1952 at year precision survives, and is now triangulated from three reported ages rather than two: 60 at his arrest on 2012-11-16, 66 at his sentencing on 2019-02-22, and 68 at his death on 2020-04-22. Those three windows intersect only between late February and April 22, 1952. The year is certain, the month is nearly so, the day is unknown.
one_case_note: He was held in two places -- the Bergen County Jail before trial and New Jersey state prison after sentencing -- but this stays one case row, because one row is what produces the single continuous span from November 16, 2012 to April 22, 2020. Splitting it would show two shorter imprisonments and lose the fact that he was never free between the two. The institution is recorded as Bergen County Jail, where he spent more than six of the seven and a half years, and which already exists in this database; the transfer to state prison is in the description. If the archive would rather see both facilities, that is a second case row and a decision about which dates split where.
name_note: The record is renamed to Roberto E. Rivera, which is how the correction identifies him, with Epifanio in the middle_name column. Flagging it because renaming to a longer form is exactly what batch 202 did to Clennon King and batch 204 had to undo: if the short form is wanted on the page, it is one field.
supersedes: The description written by batch 209, which ends by saying he is eligible for parole after seven years. He was not; he was dead. Batch 209 is merged but not yet run, so on a first run 209 writes that text and this overwrites it. Running 209 is still worth it for the state and the charges, and this batch does not depend on it.
